newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela, de Klerk differ over state of S.Africa.
newsitem.headline: Mandela, de Klerk differ over state of S.Africa.

text.p: South Africa's two most prominent politicians launched into 1997 with starkly different views on the state of their reborn nation.
President Nelson Mandela, at the helm since historic all-race elections that ended the apartheid era in April 1994, believes the country's fundamentals are sound, though tough times lie ahead.

"Across the land the impact of reconstruction and development is beginning to be felt. In short, we have laid solid foundations: the challenge for 1997 is to build on them," Mandela said in his New Year's message.
"By keeping our sights on the long term we can manage the ebbs and flows of the present," Mandela said.
But F.W. de Klerk, the last white president and the man who freed Mandela from 27 years in prison, sees the country of 42 million losing direction and heading for huge disappointment.
"The impression of a ship drifting downstream, apparently rudderless, is constantly compounded," he said in his message for 1997.

De Klerk, now leader of the white-dominated National Party which invented apartheid and then scrapped it with an apology to the five-to-one black majority four decades later, accused Mandela's government of losing its grip.
He listed as the government's worst faults "the bungling of foreign affairs and, above all, the surging crime wave".
South Africans would soon experience enormous disappointment at unfulfilled promises on education, health, development and this would haunt the government, de Klerk added.
"The expectations aroused by President Mandela and the ANC are enormous. Before long, the disappointment will take on the same proportions."

De Klerk, who was awarded the Nobel peace prize with Mandela in 1993 for their roles in South Africa's transition, led his party out of the national unity coalition government last May, saying the country had grown up enough to handle "fearless criticism" from a robust parliamentary opposition.
In this role his catalogue of woes included the ailing currency, which has lost 30 percent of its value against the dollar in less than a year.
He also cited the continued drain of "brainpower and experience" of white emigrants driven out by an ailing economy and one of the highest violent crime rates (52 murders every day) in the world.
Mandela's 1997 message was that progress had been made in redressing the skewed development that saw minority whites dominating blacks for 350 years.

"We can take pride in the fact that millions of people have gained access to water, electricity and health care; that a national education system that will afford quality education is taking shape; that land reform and our housing programmes are now firmly on track," he said.
Business Day newspaper, the country's leading financial daily, said people were now more realistic than in the heady days after the 1994 elections.
"Wish lists have given way to the realisation that not everything can be solved because we are democratic and popular and, even if it could, we do not have the money to do so.
"Expectations, both in government and among the people, are being scaled down," the paper said in an editorial.
